#: Scrub manifest for the docker collector: the three engine-API documents the adapter fetches on the acquisition path — /containers/json?all=1, /volumes and /networks — each scoped to the payload stem it answers. The engine API is the native interface, so a response document IS the payload.
#scoped: Nearly every entry names its payload, because the three documents do not share a root — containers and networks are arrays, volumes is an object — so an unscoped `*` at the root means 'a list index' in two files and 'a schema member' in the third. Scoping is what lets one manifest cover payloads with different shapes.
#shared:
Four patterns are UNSCOPED, and they have to be: a manifest is a JSON object keyed by the path pattern, so one pattern can carry one entry and therefore one scope. `*.Id`, `*.Created`, `*.Labels.*` and `*.Labels.~key` are real members of BOTH array documents — a container has an Id and a Created, and so does a network — and a second, scoped copy of any of them is simply the first key overwritten, which is a silent way to leave one document's leaves unclassified. Unscoped is the honest spelling because the classification is the same on both sides; where it would not be, this manifest could not say so, and the capture would have to be refused rather than mis-scoped.

The cost of unscoping is the `~key` entry at the volumes root below. `_keys_are_data` asks whether ANY entry walks a dict's keys with a `*`, and an unscoped `*.…` pattern does that at every document's root — including the volumes object's, whose keys are the schema's own words rather than data. So the root entry is there to answer a question the pattern language made the tool ask, and it answers it truthfully: `Volumes` and `Warnings` are member names, identical on every daemon, and they disclose nothing.
#ids: Container, image, network and endpoint ids are classified NOTHING, and the first draft of this file had them as identity — which was wrong and the tool said so, because no substitution rule engages for a 64-hex string. Correcting the classification rather than inventing a format was the answer: a docker id is minted at create time from randomness and denotes nothing outside the daemon that minted it — not a serial, not an address, not an operator's choice of name. An image DIGEST is more public still: it is a content address anyone can fetch from the registry. What made ids look identifying was that a collator joins on them, and consistency across the three documents matters — but they are consistent already, because they are captured together and published unchanged.
#nothing: Image names, OCI labels and annotations are public registry metadata, identical for everyone who pulls the same tag, and they are most of what this collection is FOR.
#argv-and-labels:
A BOUND this file needs and did not have, found by an independent audit of the first docker capture. Two members are classified `nothing` and are only safely so BECAUSE OF WHAT THIS PARTICULAR HOST RUNS, which is the shape of every subset guard this repository has had to fix.

`*.Command` is a container's argv. On this guest it is /init, `true`, and a busybox sleep loop. On a real host it is where `--api-key=`, `--password=` and `--token=` are written, because passing a secret on the command line is common and wrong and people do it anyway.

`*.Labels.*` is justified above as public registry metadata, identical for everyone who pulls the same tag. That is true of OCI labels and false of operator-written ones: traefik's `traefik.http.middlewares.<name>.basicauth.users` label carries htpasswd hashes, and this repository ships a traefik collector, so a capture from a host running Traefik behind docker would put password hashes in a public corpus under an entry that says they disclose nothing.

Neither is a leak in THIS capture. Both must be reclassified before a capture from a host running anybody's actual stacks is scrubbed — the same sentence #names already carries for container names and bind-mount paths, which these two needed and did not get.
#names:
Container, network and volume NAMES, the compose labels, and the bind-mount host paths are classified nothing FOR THIS CAPTURE, on the rule DESIGN 21 states outright — the class is a property of the VALUE, not of the field — and on the same reading harness/scrub/traefik.json already applies to its router names. Every one of them here is either docker's own vocabulary (bridge, host, none, /var/lib/docker/volumes/<volume>/_data), the image's own conventional name (radarr, prowlarr, traefik), or a word minted while staging this lab fixture (labstack, /srv/lab/…). None of them names anything in any estate.

That is a bound of this capture and NOT a property of the field, and unlike traefik's unreached members — which carry no entry, so the deny-by-default walk refuses them — a `nothing` entry here would let a future estate capture's real names and real host paths through silently. So it is stated rather than implied: a capture from a host running somebody's actual stacks carries operator-chosen names (content) and operator-chosen host paths (location), and these entries must be reclassified BEFORE that capture is scrubbed. Nothing mechanical will force it.
#empty: Docker spells 'there is no such address here' as the empty string, in seven members across two documents: Ports.*.IP on an exposed-but-unpublished port, and Gateway, IPAddress, MacAddress, IPv6Gateway and GlobalIPv6Address on a container attached to the host or null driver, and IPAM.Config.*.IPRange on every network whose operator set no range. A declared format refuses those outright — 'declared ipv4 but not an address', 'declared mac but not a MAC' — because a format asserts one shape and this member has two. So the address- and MAC-bearing members that can be empty are classified without a format and go through the free-text pass, which substitutes a real address or MAC by the same builders the format would have called and leaves the empty sentinel alone. What that costs is the format's own refusal — the check that the capture matches the declaration — and it is paid only where the sentinel makes the declaration unwritable. IPAM.Config.*.Subnet and .Gateway keep format ipv4, which is also what arms the detectors: a manifest declaring no address field reads to them as 'this file has none' rather than 'nobody looked'.
#dotted: Docker writes option and label keys with literal dots — com.docker.network.bridge.name is ONE key, not five path segments — so the dicts that hold them are classified as a whole (`Labels.*` for the values, `Labels.~key` for the keys) rather than expanded. Expanding them produced seven-segment patterns for three-segment leaves, which matched nothing and failed the walk: the deny-by-default refusal doing its job on the manifest rather than on the payload.
#unreached: The container INSPECT document (/containers/{id}/json) carries Env, where an operator's secrets live and which the adapter redacts on the way out. Inspect is reached by get_object and get_evidence, never by acquire, so it is outside this corpus — and the deny-by-default walk is what will force this file to grow before an inspect payload can ever be committed. Nothing here classifies an IPv6-enabled network either: EnableIPv6 is false on every network this daemon carries, so the GlobalIPv6Address and IPv6Gateway members are only ever seen holding the empty sentinel.
